title: Plan 9 from Outer Space

evidence.note: A web search turned up a report that Wade Williams claims to own the copyright, having renewed it in 1986. The same source says the film's ownership has been questioned. Earlier research recorded the renewal number RE0000279707. We could not confirm that number or open the renewal record in this session, because the Copyright Office catalog cannot be searched automatically. We found no court ruling or Copyright Office decision that settles whether any renewal is valid. The Public Domain Review lists the film as public domain, but it cites no renewal search. Because the renewal question is unresolved, this layer stays undetermined.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System

evidence.note: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Parts 12-13: Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan-Dec 1958 (archive.org identifier catalogofcopyrig3121213li). We confirmed the volume's title and year on its archive.org page. We did not search its text for this film. The volume covers original registrations, not renewals, so it does not settle the question.
evidence.source: Internet Archive / Library of Congress Copyright Office

evidence.note: The recorded soundtrack as embodied in the film follows the film's own copyright status, which is undetermined (see the print layer). Individual musical compositions on the soundtrack may have separate copyright histories. Check each one before licensing it for new synchronization or commercial release.

Ed Wood wrote and directed the film. We found nothing showing it was adapted from an earlier published work, so the story takes the film's own status. That status is undetermined because of the renewal question described in the print layer.

USPTO trademark databases could not be searched automatically in this session. We know of no active mark for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space', but trademark status stays undetermined until a USPTO search is done.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions such as a new score, colorization, or new titles and subtitles can be protected. Colorized versions of this film are reported to exist, and colorization is protected on its own. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Plan 9 from Outer Space is an Ed Wood science-fiction horror film. Wood wrote and directed it. Extraterrestrials try to stop humans from building a doomsday weapon by resurrecting the dead. Bela Lugosi gets posthumous billing, using silent footage Wood shot before Lugosi died in 1956 for other unfinished projects. A creator might want it for its cult reputation and its place in 'worst film ever made' lore. The Internet Archive hosts it and the Public Domain Review lists it as public domain.

The rights trap is the renewal. A search turned up a report that Wade Williams claims to own the copyright, having renewed it in 1986. Earlier research recorded the renewal number RE0000279707, which we could not re-confirm. Some commentators doubt Williams's ownership. We found no ruling that settles the point. Treat the film as possibly still protected, and get advice before reusing footage commercially.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. Wade Williams is reported to claim a 1986 renewal, and earlier research recorded the number RE0000279707. Some doubt its validity, but we found no ruling that settles it, so the status is undetermined. Get advice before reusing footage.
Is a colorized version of Plan 9 public domain too?

No. Colorization adds new creative authorship that is protected on its own, whatever the status of the original black-and-white film. A colorized copy may be off-limits even if the original turns out to be free to use.
